s0002:
Malika wants to make a yogurt dressing for a salad for her guests. The recipe in her cookbook is for 200 milliliters (ml) of dressing:

Yogurt — 120 ml
Lemon juice — 50 ml
Olive oil — 30 ml

Because there are many guests, Malika needs more dressing.
s0003: Scaling up a recipe using a ratio (proportion)
s0004: First find how many times larger the new amount is than the old one, then multiply each ingredient by that number.
s0005: Malika wants to make 300 ml of dressing using this recipe. How many milliliters of yogurt will she need?
s0007: The dressing needed is 1.5 times the amount in the recipe.
s0009: Each ingredient is also multiplied by 1.5, so the yogurt is 180 ml.
s0011: The lemon juice is 75 ml and the oil is 45 ml, 300 ml in total — correct.
s0014: A common mistake is to add 100 ml to the yogurt because 100 ml is being added to the total (220 ml), or to add 50 to 120. To keep the ratio the same, every ingredient is multiplied by the same number.
s0015: When a recipe is scaled up, you do not add to the ingredients; you multiply them all by the same factor.
s0017:
In a city park, a large Ferris wheel has been built on the bank of the Ankhor canal (see the drawing).

The outer diameter of the Ferris wheel is 60 meters, and its highest point is 66 meters above the water level. The lowest point P is next to the boarding platform, 6 meters above the water level. The wheel turns in the direction shown by the arrow in the drawing: P → Q → R → S → P.
s0020: Calculating a length from information in a drawing (diameter, radius, height)
s0021: The center is one radius below the highest point. Half of the diameter is the radius.
s0022: In the drawing, the letter M marks the center of the Ferris wheel. How many meters above the water level is point M?
s0023: The radius is half the diameter — 30 meters.
s0024: The center is one radius below the highest point.
s0026: Going one radius up from the lowest point also gives 36 m.
s0028: Point M is 36 meters above the water level.
s0029: A common mistake is 66 − 60 = 6 (subtracting the diameter) or 66 : 2 = 33 (dividing the height in half). It cannot be 33 m, because the wheel starts 6 m above the water.
s0030: The center is halfway between the highest and lowest points: (66 + 6) : 2.
s0031: Finding a position over time in uniform rotation (a fraction of a circle)
s0032: Find what fraction of a full turn the given time is, and mark that fraction in the direction of rotation.
s0033: The Ferris wheel turns at a constant speed and makes one full turn in exactly 24 minutes. Sardor got into a cabin at point P. Where will Sardor be 18 minutes later?
s0038: 18 minutes is three quarters of a full turn.
s0039: With every quarter turn, the cabin reaches the next letter: Q, R, S.
s0040: In 18 minutes: P → Q → R → S
s0041: After three quarters, Sardor will be exactly at point S.
s0044: Point R is reached after half a turn (12 minutes); after 18 minutes the cabin has already gone past it.
s0045: The cabin is between R and S from minute 12 to minute 18; at minute 18 it reaches S exactly.
s0046: Between S and P corresponds to the time between 18 and 24 minutes; in that case the time would have to be more than 3/4 of a turn.
s0047: Write the time as a fraction: 18/24 = 3/4 — that is three quarters of a turn.
s0049:
On a table, Jasur built a structure with four columns out of 7 identical dice (the drawing shows the front view). The heights of the columns: column 1 has 2 dice, column 2 has 1, column 3 has 3, and column 4 has 1 die.

On a standard die, the dots on opposite faces always add up to 7 (1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4).

Before placing the top die of each column, Jasur wrote down the number of dots on its bottom face (the face touching the die below or the table):
Column 1: 2 dots
Column 2: 6 dots
Column 3: 3 dots
Column 4: 4 dots
s0059: Visualizing a 3D structure from another side (from above)
s0060: From above, only the top die of each column can be seen. Its top face is opposite its bottom face: top = 7 − bottom.
s0061: How many dots in total can be seen when the structure is viewed from above?
s0063: Only the top die of each column is visible; the other 3 are hidden.
s0065: Opposite faces add up to 7, so we find the top face.
s0068: In total, 13 dots are visible from above.
s0069: Common mistakes: adding the bottom faces (2+6+3+4 = 15) or counting all 7 dice. From above, only 4 top faces are visible, and they are opposite the bottom faces.
s0070: First count how many dice are visible from above, then for each one subtract the bottom face from 7.
s0072: Greater Chimgan is a famous peak in the Tashkent Region (3309 m high). The hiking trail to the top is open to tourists only in summer. The numbers in the questions below are approximate and are used for learning purposes.
s0073: Finding a daily average from a total and a range of dates
s0074: First count exactly how many days are in the date range (take into account the number of days in each month), then divide the total by the number of days.
s0075: Every year the trail is open from July 1 to August 31 (both days included). During this period, about 31 000 people climb to the peak. About how many people climb it per day on average?
s0077: First we count how many days the trail is open.
s0078: We divide the total by the number of days.
s0080: On average, 500 people climb it per day.
s0081: 50 — a place value was lost in the division (31 000 : 620).
s0082: 1000 is the result of dividing 31 000 by the 31 days of only one month, but the trail is open for two months.
s0083: 15 500 is the number of people per month (31 000 : 2), not per day.
s0084: If the question asks “per day”, the divisor is the number of days, not months.
s0085: Finding a start time from two different speeds, a distance and an end time
s0086: Calculate the time going up and the time coming down separately (t = s : v), add them, and count back from the end time.
s0087: The trail to the peak is about 6 km long. Hikers on the 12 km round-trip hike must be back by 19:00. Aziz estimates that he will walk up at an average speed of 1.2 km per hour and come down twice as fast (these speeds include time for rest and meals). What is the latest time Aziz can start the hike to be back by 19:00? (Write the answer as hours:minutes, like 08:15.)
s0090: For the time going up, we divide the distance by the speed.
s0092: The speed coming down is twice as high, so the time is half as long.
s0094: The whole hike takes seven and a half hours.
s0095: We count back from the end time.
s0097: Aziz must set off at 11:30 at the latest.
s0098: Common mistakes: dividing 12 km by one speed (12 : 1.2 = 10 hours → 09:00), taking the speed coming down as slower instead of twice as fast, or reading 7.5 hours as 7 hours 50 minutes.
s0099: 0.5 hours = 30 minutes. Calculate the times going up and coming down separately.
s0100: Dividing a length given in kilometers and converting the result to centimeters
s0101: First convert the distance to centimeters (1 km = 100 000 cm), then divide by the number of steps.
s0102: Aziz wore a step counter (pedometer) on the hike. On the 6 km trail to the peak, the pedometer showed 12 000 steps. What was Aziz's average step length on the way up, in centimeters?
s0105: We convert the distance to centimeters right away.
s0106: We divide the distance by the number of steps.
s0108: With half-meter steps we get 6 km — it matches.
s0110: The average step length is 50 cm.
s0111: Often the answer is left in meters (0.5) or the units are converted incorrectly (5 or 5000). Remember that 1 m = 100 cm and 1 km = 1000 m.
s0112: Check whether the result is realistic: an adult's step is usually 40–80 cm.
s0114: Dilnoza was given a new bicycle. There is a speedometer on the handlebars: it shows the distance traveled and the average speed for the trip.
s0115: Comparing average speeds using distance and time
s0116: Calculate the speed for each part in the same units (for example, km/h), or compare the ratios of distance and time.
s0117: On one trip, Dilnoza rode 3 km in the first 12 minutes and 1.5 km in the next 6 minutes. Which of the following statements is correct?
s0118: Dilnoza's average speed was greater in the first 12 minutes than in the next 6 minutes.
s0119: Dilnoza's average speed was the same in the first 12 minutes and in the next 6 minutes.
s0120: Dilnoza's average speed was smaller in the first 12 minutes than in the next 6 minutes.
s0121: Nothing can be said about the average speed from the given information.
s0123: 12 minutes is one fifth of an hour: 3 · 5 = 15.
s0125: 6 minutes is one tenth of an hour: 1.5 · 10 = 15.
s0127: Half the distance in half the time — the speed did not change.
s0130: 3 km is more than 1.5 km, but the time is also twice as long — you cannot compare speeds using distance alone.
s0131: 6 minutes is a short time, but the distance is also half as long, so the speed neither decreased nor increased.
s0132: The distance and time are known — the average speed can be calculated exactly.
s0133: Speed = distance : time. If both the distance and the time change by a factor of two, the speed does not change.
s0134: Calculating time from average speed and distance
s0135: Time = distance : speed. Convert the result from hours to minutes (1 hour = 60 minutes).
s0136: Dilnoza rode 5 km to her grandmother's house. The speedometer showed that her average speed for the whole trip was 20 km/h. Which of the following statements is correct?
s0137: Dilnoza got to her grandmother's house in 4 hours.
s0138: Dilnoza got to her grandmother's house in 15 minutes.
s0139: Dilnoza got to her grandmother's house in 25 minutes.
s0140: It is impossible to determine how long it took Dilnoza to get to her grandmother's house.
s0142: To find the time, we divide the distance by the speed.
s0144: A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes.
s0146: 4 hours is the result of dividing the speed by the distance (20 : 5); at that rate the cyclist would have been very slow.
s0147: 25 minutes is the result of adding 5 and 20; adding the numbers does not give the time.
s0148: If the average speed and the distance are known, the time can be found exactly.
s0149: Look at the units: if you divide km by km/h, you get hours.
s0150: Calculating the average speed for a two-part journey from the total distance and total time
s0151: Average speed = total distance : total time. Do not take the arithmetic mean of the two speeds.
s0152: Dilnoza rode her bicycle to the bazaar, 5 km from her home, in 12 minutes. She came home by a shorter 4 km route, which took 8 minutes. What was Dilnoza's average speed for the round trip to the bazaar, in km/h?
s0155: We add up the distance for the whole trip.
s0157: The total time is 20 minutes, which is one third of an hour.
s0159: We divide the total distance by the total time.
s0162: A common mistake is to take the average of the two speeds: 25 km/h going there and 30 km/h coming back, (25 + 30) : 2 = 27.5. This is wrong, because the parts have different distances and times.
s0163: Always calculate average speed as “total distance : total time”.
s0165:
Kamola is thinking of buying a holiday apartment near the Charvak Reservoir and renting it out to vacationers. An online listing (made up):

Price: 520 million soums
Rooms: 1 living room with kitchen, 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom
Area: 48 m²
Parking: yes
Travel time to the village center: 12 minutes
Distance to the water (in a straight line): 800 m
Average number of days booked by vacationers over the last 8 years: 240 days per year
s0166: Calculating a value using a table of several criteria and comparing it with a price
s0167: For each criterion, determine which column the value from the listing falls into, then add the base price and the extras.
s0168:
Kamola contacted a professional appraiser. The appraiser calculates the value of the apartment using the following criteria:

Base price: 9 million soums per 1 m².
Travel time to the center: more than 15 minutes — +0; from 5 to 15 minutes — +20 million; less than 5 minutes — +40 million soums.
Distance to the water (straight line): more than 2 km — +0; 1–2 km — +10 million; 0.5–1 km — +25 million; less than 0.5 km — +40 million soums.
Parking: no — +0; yes — +50 million soums.

If the appraiser's valuation is higher than the price in the listing, the price is considered “very good” for the buyer.

According to the appraiser's criteria, what is the value of the apartment in millions of soums? (Write only the number.)
s0171: Base price: we multiply the area by the price per 1 m².
s0173: 12 minutes is in the 5–15 range, and 800 m is in the 0.5–1 km range.
s0175: There is also an extra amount for parking.
s0176: The valuation is 527 million, which is more than the 520 million in the listing — the price is “very good”.
s0178: The appraiser's valuation is 527 million soums.
s0179: Common mistakes: putting 800 m in the “less than 0.5 km” column (+40), forgetting one of the extras, or stopping at 48 · 9 = 432. Mark each criterion separately.
s0180: 800 m = 0.8 km. Find each criterion in the table separately and write them down as a list.
s0181: Understanding what an average means and what it does not guarantee
s0182: The average is the number you would get if the total days were shared equally among the years. Individual years can be above or below it; if some years are above the average, others must be below it.
s0183:
“240 days per year on average” is the average number of booked days over the last 8 years (assume a year has 365 days).

1) It can be said for certain that in at least one year the apartment was booked for exactly 240 days.
2) In theory, the apartment could have been booked for more than 240 days in each of the last 8 years.
3) In theory, the apartment could have had no bookings at all in one of the last 8 years.

Does each statement follow from the given information (“Yes”) or not (“No”)? Choose the row with the correct answers.
s0189: If the average is 240, the total number of booked days over 8 years is 1920.
s0190: 1) No: for example, years with 230 and 250 days
s0191: The average can be 240 even if no single year is exactly 240.
s0193: If every year were more than 240, the average would also be more than 240.
s0195: The other 7 years can easily cover the 1920 days.
s0198: Statement 1 is not guaranteed: even if the average is 240, it is possible that no year is exactly 240; and statement 3 is possible.
s0199: Statement 2 is impossible: if all years were more than 240, the average would also be more than 240.
s0200: Statements 1 and 2 are false and statement 3 is true — this row has everything the other way around.
s0201: Think of the average as “total : number of years” and check each statement against the total of 1920 days.

Bekzod goes to the swimming pool in his mahalla. A yearly membership card for the pool costs 80 000 soums. Members pay less for each visit than non-members:

Price per visit (non-member): 15 000 soums
Price per visit (member): 12 000 soums
s0204: Calculating and comparing numbers in an everyday situation
s0205: First subtract the membership card and find the number of visits; then multiply that number by the non-member price.
s0206: Last year Bekzod was a member of the pool. During the year he spent a total of 560 000 soums, including the membership card. If he had not been a member and had gone to the pool the same number of times, how many soums would he have spent?
s0208: First we subtract the price of the membership card.
s0210: The rest of the money was spent on visits — 40 visits.
s0211: Without membership, each visit costs 15 000 soums.
s0214: Common mistakes: calculating 560 000 : 12 000 without subtracting the membership card, or writing the number of visits (40) as the answer. The question asks for the total cost without membership.
s0215: Total cost = card + visits. First find the number of visits.
s0216: Comparing two ways of paying and finding the smallest whole number for which one is cheaper
s0217: Find the savings per visit and divide the price of the card by those savings; round the result to a whole number that makes sense in the situation.
s0218: What is the minimum number of times a person must go to the pool in a year for membership to pay off (that is, for a member to pay less than a non-member)?
s0221: On each visit, a member saves 3000 soums.
s0222: To cover the price of the card, 26.7 visits are needed.
s0224: With 26 visits, a member still pays more.
s0226: With 27 visits, a member pays less.
s0227: You need to go at least 27 times.
s0228: A common mistake is to round 26.7 down and say 26. The number of visits must be a whole number, and to get a benefit you need to round up; with 26 visits a member still pays 2000 soums more.
s0229: After rounding, check your answer with both prices.
s0231:
The table gives information about households with a TV in five areas. It also shows how many of the households with a TV subscribe to internet television (IPTV). The numbers were made up for learning purposes and are approximate.

Area | Households with a TV | Households with a TV as a share of all households | IPTV subscribers as a share of households with a TV
Tashkent City | 720 thousand | 98.5% | 46.0%
Samarkand Region | 880 thousand | 96.0% | 12.5%
Fergana Region | 810 thousand | 97.0% | 15.0%
Khorezm Region | 390 thousand | 95.5% | 18.0%
Navoi Region | 240 thousand | 85.0% | 62.5%
s0232: Finding the whole from a percentage (proportion) using data in a table
s0233: Households with a TV are 85% of all households. To find the whole from a part, divide the part by the percentage written as a decimal.
s0234: According to the table, 85.0% of all households in the Navoi Region have a TV. Which is the closest estimate of the total number of households in the Navoi Region?
s0240: 240 thousand is 85 percent of all households.
s0242: To find the whole, we divide.
s0244: There must be more households in total than households with a TV — it matches.
s0246: 204 thousand is the result of multiplying 240 by 0.85; this number is smaller than 240, but the whole must be larger than the part.
s0247: 255 thousand is as if 15 thousand, not 15%, were added to 240; the percentage must be applied correctly.
s0248: 325 thousand is too large: 85% of 325 is 276 thousand, not 240 thousand.
s0249: If a part is given as a percentage, whole = part : (percentage/100). The whole is always larger than the part.
s0250: Telling percentages and absolute numbers apart; understanding what whole a percentage refers to
s0251: To find the number of subscribers, multiply the percentage by the correct whole — the number of households with a TV — and compare.
s0252:
Looking at the Fergana and Khorezm regions, Otabek said: “In both regions the percentage of households with a TV is almost the same, and the IPTV percentage is higher in Khorezm. So more households subscribe to IPTV in Khorezm than in Fergana.”

Why is Otabek's reasoning wrong? Choose the best explanation.
s0253: The reasoning is wrong because the percentage of households with a TV in Fergana (97.0%) is higher than in Khorezm (95.5%).
s0254: The reasoning is wrong because the difference between 18% and 15% is only 3%, which is negligible.
s0255: The reasoning is wrong because the percentages refer to households with a TV, and Fergana has many more such households: about 121.5 thousand versus 70.2 thousand subscribers.
s0256: The reasoning is correct because 18% is greater than 15%.
s0258: We calculate the number of subscribers in Fergana.
s0260: In Khorezm the percentage is higher, but the whole is much smaller.
s0262: Fergana has more subscribers — Otabek made a mistake.
s0263: Answer: C) the percentages are of different wholes
s0265: The difference of 1.5 percentage points (97.0 and 95.5) is not decisive here; the main reason is the large difference in the number of households with a TV.
s0266: Calling a 3-point difference negligible is also wrong: even when the percentages are equal, the number of subscribers depends on the whole.
s0267: Otabek's reasoning is wrong: even though the percentage is higher, 18 percent of a small whole is less than 15 percent of a large whole.
s0268: Before comparing percentages, always ask: “This is a percentage — of what?”

Shahzoda has just got her driver's license and wants to buy her first car. At a car dealership she saw four used cars (the model names are made up):

Model | Lola | Bahor | Sayyor | Tulpor
Year made | 2019 | 2017 | 2018 | 2016
Price (million soums) | 98 | 89 | 86 | 79
Mileage (km) | 85 000 | 92 000 | 118 000 | 88 000
Engine size (liters) | 1.49 | 1.496 | 1.52 | 1.487
s0271: Choosing an item from a table that meets several conditions at the same time
s0272: Check each condition in turn and cross out the ones that do not meet it.
s0285: Only Bahor meets all three conditions.
s0286: Lola is the newest and has the lowest mileage, but its price is 98 million — more than 90 million.
s0287: Sayyor is cheaper, but it has 118 000 km on it — more than 100 000 km.
s0288: Tulpor is the cheapest, but it was made in 2016 — before 2017.
s0289: Check the conditions one by one: if a car fails one condition, it is out.
s0290: Comparing decimals and finding the smallest
s0291: Write the decimals with the same number of decimal places (1.490; 1.496; 1.520; 1.487) and compare them place by place.
s0292: Which car has the smallest engine size?
s0293: We write all the numbers as decimals with three decimal places.
s0294: Ones and tenths: all are 1.4.. or 1.5..
s0295: 1.520 is the largest — it is out.
s0299: Tulpor has the smallest engine size.
s0300: 1.49 looks small because it is written with fewer digits, but it equals 1.490 and is greater than 1.487.
s0301: 1.496 has more digits, but a longer number is not necessarily larger or smaller: 1.496 > 1.487.
s0302: 1.52 is the largest number, because it has 5 in the tenths place.
s0303: When comparing decimals, add zeros at the end to make the number of decimal places equal.
s0304: Calculating a percentage (a decimal percentage) of a large number
s0305: 3.5% = 0.035. Multiply the price by 0.035, or first find 1% and then 3.5%.
s0306: To register the car, Shahzoda must pay an extra fee equal to 3.5% of its price. How many soums will the extra fee be for the Lola car?
s0309: We write the price in soums.
s0311: We divide by one hundred to find one percent.
s0315: Common mistakes: taking 3.5% as 0.35 (34 300 000) or writing 98 · 3.5 = 343 as soums. The answer is asked for in soums; 3.43 million soums is also correct.
s0316: Converting a percentage to a decimal: 3.5% = 3.5 : 100 = 0.035.
s0318:
A company makes “basic” prefabricated sheds: they have only one door and one window. The door is always in the front wall with the triangular gable, and the window is in one of the side walls.

Ravshan chose a shed of this type for his yard. The drawing shows its front view and its right side view: the door is in the front wall, and the window is in the back part of the right side wall.
s0319: Spatial visualization: working out how an object looks from another side based on one view
s0320: Imagine walking around the object to the back: the right side wall now appears on the left, and the back wall is the closest to you.
s0321: The pictures below show “basic” sheds from the back (so that the back wall and one side wall are visible). Only one of them matches the shed Ravshan chose. Which one?
s0322: From the back: back gable has no door
s0323: The door is in the front wall, so no door is visible in the back wall.
s0324: The right side wall is now on the left
s0325: When you walk around to the back, right and left swap.
s0326: The window is close to the back wall
s0327: The window is in the back part of the side wall — next to the back gable.
s0329: All these conditions are met only in picture D.
s0330: A is a copy of the front view without a door: the side wall stays on the right, but when viewed from the back it should be on the left.
s0331: In B the side wall is on the correct side, but the window is far from the back wall — it is in the front part.
s0332: In C the side wall is on the right, which is the side of the left wall that should have no window.
s0333: Take a paper box in your hands and turn it around: the right side appears on the left when you look from the back.
s0334: Reading dimensions from a drawing, finding the width of a roof with the Pythagorean theorem and calculating area
s0335: The width of one slope of the roof is the hypotenuse of a right triangle (legs: half the width and the height of the roof). Then find the area of the rectangle and double it.
s0336: The drawing gives the dimensions (in meters) of the shed Ravshan chose. The roof consists of two identical rectangular pieces. Find the total area of the roof (in m²).
s0339: Dimensions in meters. Not to scale.
s0341: The roof slope is in a triangle made of half the width, 2.40 m, and the height, 0.70 m.
s0343: The width of one roof piece is 2.5 meters.
s0344: Two pieces, each 6.40 m by 2.5 m.
s0346: The total area of the roof is 32 m².
s0347: Common mistakes: using half the width instead of the slope (2 · 2.40 · 6.40 = 30.72), forgetting to double (16), or adding 2.40 + 0.70 = 3.1. The length of a slanted line is found with the Pythagorean theorem.
s0348: In the front view, draw a right triangle with the roof slope as its hypotenuse.
s0350:
Two delivery services in the city (the names are made up) are hiring couriers. Their ads say how the pay works:

“FAST DELIVERY”: Need extra income? Each week we pay 3000 soums for each of the first 40 orders, and 5000 soums for every order after that.

“EASY COURIER”: Less time — good income! A fixed 150 000 soums per week plus an extra 1500 soums for each order.
s0351: Calculating income in a piecewise (two-rate) payment model
s0352: Split the orders into two parts: the first 40 and the rest; multiply each part by its own rate.
s0353: Ulugbek delivers an average of 55 orders per week for “Fast Delivery”. How many soums does he earn per week on average?
s0356: The first 40 orders are paid at the lower rate.
s0358: Another 15 orders are paid at the higher rate.
s0363: Common mistakes: multiplying all the orders by one rate (55 · 3000 = 165 000 or 55 · 5000 = 275 000) or calculating 40 · 3000 + 55 · 5000. The higher rate applies only to the orders after the first 40.
s0364: Count the “first 40” orders and the “later” orders separately.
s0365: Finding an unknown quantity from a linear model (working backward)
s0366: Subtract the fixed part from the income and divide the rest by the pay per order.
s0367: Nodira works for “Easy Courier”. In one week she earned 240 000 soums. How many orders did she deliver that week?
s0369: Income = fixed pay + pay for orders.
s0371: We divide by the pay per order.
s0374: A common mistake is to calculate 240 000 : 1500 = 160 without subtracting the fixed 150 000 soums.
s0375: First subtract the fixed part, then divide. Check your answer: 150 000 + 60 · 1500.
s0376: Recognizing two linear relationships on a graph (starting value, slope, break point)
s0377: For each service: what is the income for 0 orders (where does the graph start)? Is the slope the same throughout, or does it change somewhere?
s0378: Javohir wants to choose which service to work for. Which of the following graphs correctly shows how the two services pay couriers? (Solid line — “Easy Courier”, dashed line — “Fast Delivery”.)
s0384: There is fixed pay, so the line starts above zero and rises right away.
s0386: If there are no orders, “Fast Delivery” pays nothing.
s0388: After 40 orders, each order pays more — the graph bends and rises more steeply.
s0390: All three features appear only in graph B.
s0391: In A, the “Easy Courier” line is horizontal at the start; but each order immediately adds 1500 soums, so there should be no flat part.
s0392: In C, the “Fast Delivery” line is straight; in fact, the pay increases after 40 orders and the line bends.
s0393: D has both mistakes: “Easy Courier” is flat at the start, and “Fast Delivery” does not bend.
s0394: Two features to check on a graph: the starting point (the value at 0) and the place where the slope changes.
s0395: Revolving Door at a Shopping Mall
s0396:
A revolving door has been installed at the entrance of a shopping mall. It consists of four wings that turn inside a circular space. The inner diameter of the space is 240 cm. The four wings divide the space into four equal sectors.

On the edge of the circle there are two fixed walls (the left and right arcs), and between them there are two identical openings: one on the entrance side and one on the exit side (the dashed arcs in the drawing). The drawing shows the door from above.
s0403: Calculating the central angle when a circle is divided into equal sectors
s0404: A full turn is 360°. Divide by the number of equal sectors.
s0405: How many degrees is the angle between two neighboring wings?
s0407: The wings divide the full circle around the center.
s0408: Four equal sectors — each is 90 degrees.
s0410: The angle between neighboring wings is 90°.
s0411: Common mistakes: dividing 360 by 3 (120°) or dividing 180 by 4 (45°). The wings come out of the center and divide the whole circle — 360° — equally.

s0413: Interpreting a geometric model and calculating an arc length
s0414: To keep air from passing through, each wall must be able to fully close off at least one sector. The two walls and the two openings together make up 360°. Find the angle of an opening and calculate the arc length as a fraction of the circumference.
s0415: If the openings are too wide, the wings cannot form a closed space: some sector will be open to both the entrance and the exit sides at the same time, and air will flow freely from the street inside (heat is lost). For air never to flow freely from the entrance to the exit, what is the maximum length, in centimeters, of the arc of each opening? (Use π ≈ 3.14 and round your answer to the nearest whole number.)
s0417: A wall must close off at least one sector; otherwise a sector touches both openings.
s0419: On the edge of the circle there are two openings and two walls.
s0421: So each opening is at most 90°.
s0423: 90° is a quarter of the circle: 3.14 · 240 : 4.
s0425: The arc of each opening is at most about 188 cm.
s0426: Common mistakes: writing the sum of both openings (377 cm), mixing up the radius and the diameter (94 cm), or simply writing the radius (120 cm) as the answer. Each opening is a quarter of the circle — a 90° arc.

s0428: Selecting data and building a hidden quantitative model (turns, sectors, time)
s0429: Find how many sectors pass the entrance in one turn and how many people fit in each; then multiply by the turns per minute and by the time.
s0430: The door makes 3 full turns per minute. Each of the four sectors holds at most 2 people. What is the greatest number of people who can enter the building through the door in 20 minutes?
s0432: In one turn, each of the four sectors passes the entrance once.
